where: Every glass you drink, every cloud, and about 60 % of you.
On food, and dissolved in your blood, your sweat and the sea.
In every breath you breathe out, and in the bubbles of a fizzy drink.
About a fifth of the air: the part your lungs are after.
About four fifths of every breath, passing in and out unused.
The sugar in your blood, made by plants from sunlight, and the fuel your cells burn.
The white sugar in the bowl, pressed from sugar cane or beet.
The gas that burns on a gas stove, and what cows and swamps give off.
Eggshells, seashells, chalk, limestone and marble.
Most of the sand on a beach, and the raw stuff of glass.
On old bikes and nails, and the red in red soil and on Mars.
The alcohol in wine and beer, made by yeast eating sugar.
What makes vinegar sour: about 5 % of it, the rest is water.
In cakes and bread, where it gives off carbon dioxide bubbles when it meets an acid.
In coffee, tea and chocolate, where plants make it to put off insects.
The sour in lemons and limes.
The sharp smell in some glass cleaners, and the start of most fertiliser.
Household bleach: a few percent of it dissolved in water.
The lightest gas; most of the Sun, and a fuel that burns to plain water.
Nearly 1 % of the air you breathe, passing through untouched.
High in the sky, where a thin layer of it blocks most of the Sun's harshest light.
In working muscles, and the tang in yoghurt and sourdough.
How your body gets rid of spare nitrogen, in urine; also a farm fertiliser.
The simplest amino acid: a building block of every protein in you.
The "A" of DNA's four letters, in every cell you have.
The hard part of your bones, and almost all of your tooth enamel.
Made by roasting limestone; the start of cement and mortar.
The bright white in most paint, toothpaste and mineral sunscreen.
Ruby and sapphire are this, coloured by a trace of another metal; and the same oxide forms the thin skin on aluminium foil.
A black iron ore that is naturally magnetic: the first compasses used it.
Shiny gold-coloured cubes in rock, called fool's gold.
The rotten-egg smell of volcanoes and hot springs.
Bridges, cars, rails, knives: the most used metal there is.
Statues, bells and medals; the first alloy people made, about 5,000 years ago.
A gas used to push the spray out of some aerosol cans.
A mild bleach and disinfectant, fizzing on a cut.
From fires and engines that burn without enough air; poisonous and without smell.
The brown haze of city smog, from hot engines.
A yellow-green gas used to keep pools and tap water free of germs.
In car batteries, and the most made chemical in industry.
why: Oxygen shares a pair of electrons with each hydrogen, and its other electrons push the two hydrogens into a bent shape.
Sodium hands one electron to chlorine; the two end up with opposite charges, and opposite charges cling.
Carbon shares two pairs of electrons with each oxygen (a double bond), so the three atoms sit in a straight line.
An oxygen atom is two electrons short of a full outer shell, so two of them share two pairs and both are satisfied.
Two nitrogens share three pairs of electrons (a triple bond), one of the strongest bonds there is, so the gas barely reacts.
Carbon atoms share electrons in a ring with one oxygen, and the hydrogens and other oxygens hang off its sides.
Two smaller sugar rings, glucose and fructose, are joined through a shared oxygen atom.
Carbon shares one pair of electrons with each of four hydrogens, which spread out as far apart as they can, like a tripod with a mast.
Calcium hands two electrons to a carbonate group (one carbon sharing electrons with three oxygens), and the charges cling.
Each silicon shares electrons with four oxygens, and each oxygen bridges two silicons, so the whole crystal is one web.
Forms when iron meets water and air over time: iron hands electrons to oxygen, and the charged atoms pack into a crystal.
Two carbons share a bond, and the oxygen sits at one end holding a hydrogen, which lets it mix with water.
Two carbons share a bond; one holds two oxygens, and the hydrogen on one of them comes away easily in water, which is what makes it an acid.
Sodium hands one electron to a bicarbonate group (carbon, oxygen and hydrogen sharing electrons), and the charges cling.
Carbon and nitrogen atoms share electrons in two joined rings, with oxygens and small carbon groups on the edges.
A short carbon chain shares electrons with three acid groups, each with a hydrogen that comes away in water.
Nitrogen shares one pair of electrons with each of three hydrogens; its spare pair pushes them into a low pyramid.
Sodium hands one electron to a hypochlorite group (chlorine sharing electrons with oxygen), which grabs electrons from stains and germs.
Each hydrogen has one electron; two of them share their electrons as a pair, and both are satisfied.
Its outer shell of electrons is already full, so it has nothing to share or hand over.
Three oxygens share electrons in a bent chain; the bonds are strained, so ozone breaks apart easily.
A three-carbon chain shares electrons with an acid group at one end, whose hydrogen comes away in water.
One carbon shares a double bond with oxygen and single bonds with two nitrogens, each holding two hydrogens.
Two carbons share a bond; one carries a nitrogen group, the other an acid group, and those ends link amino acids into chains.
Carbons and nitrogens share electrons in two joined rings, flat like a tile, which lets it stack inside DNA.
Calcium hands electrons to phosphate groups (phosphorus sharing electrons with four oxygens) and to hydroxide (an oxygen holding a hydrogen).
Calcium hands two electrons to oxygen, and the two charged atoms stack like table salt.
Titanium hands electrons to two oxygens, and the charged atoms pack tightly into a crystal that scatters light.
Aluminium hands electrons to oxygen, and the tightly packed charged atoms make one of the hardest minerals.
Iron hands electrons to oxygen in two different amounts, two or three each, and the mix packs into a magnetic crystal.
Iron hands electrons to pairs of sulfur atoms, which share electrons with each other, and the crystal grows as cubes.
Like water, with sulfur in oxygen's place: sulfur shares a pair of electrons with each hydrogen, in a bent shape.
Iron atoms share a sea of loose electrons; small carbon atoms tucked between them stop the layers sliding, so it is much harder than iron.
Copper and tin atoms share a sea of loose electrons; the bigger tin atoms jam the layers, so bronze is harder than either.
The oxygen sits between two carbons and holds no hydrogen of its own, so unlike ethanol it boils away below freezing.
Water with one more oxygen: two oxygens share a weak bond, which breaks easily and gives off oxygen.
Carbon and oxygen share three pairs of electrons; it clings to your blood more tightly than oxygen does.
Nitrogen shares electrons with two oxygens but is left with one unpaired electron, which makes it eager to react.
Each chlorine is one electron short of a full outer shell, so two of them share one pair.
Sulfur shares electrons with four oxygens; two of them hold hydrogens that come away in water, which makes it a strong acid.
note: There is no single salt molecule: sodium and chloride ions (charged atoms) stack into a cube, millions at a time.
An element can pair with itself: the oxygen you breathe is two oxygen atoms bonded together.
It forms a crystal, not single molecules: calcium ions and carbonate groups stack in a repeating pattern.
There is no single SiO₂ molecule: the bonds go on in every direction, which is why quartz is so hard.
Two iron to three oxygen is the ratio in which the charges balance.
Same atoms, different shape: dimethyl ether is also C₂H₆O, with the oxygen in the middle, and it is a gas.
A crystal of sodium ions and bicarbonate groups, not single molecules.
As a solid it is a crystal of ions (charged atoms); you meet it dissolved.
An element can pair with itself: hydrogen gas is two hydrogen atoms bonded together.
Argon stays on its own: noble gases (the last column) almost never combine.
The same element, a different count: three oxygens make ozone, two make the oxygen you breathe.
The first body chemical made in a lab (1828), which showed life's molecules follow the same rules as everything else.
A calcium phosphate crystal. Bone grows tiny crystals of it on a mesh of protein, which is why bone is hard but not brittle.
A crystal of calcium and oxide ions (charged atoms), with the same cube pattern as table salt.
A crystal, not single molecules.
Two aluminium to three oxygen is the ratio in which the charges balance.
Like rust, but with less oxygen: three iron to four oxygen.
The cube-shaped crystals you can find in rock are the lattice, grown large.
Steel has no fixed formula: it is iron with up to about 2 % carbon. A mix of metals like this is an alloy, not a compound.
Bronze has no fixed formula: usually about nine parts copper to one of tin. An alloy is a mix, not a compound.
Same atoms, different shape: ethanol is also C₂H₆O, with the oxygen at the end, and it is a liquid.
An element can pair with itself: chlorine gas is two chlorine atoms bonded together.
